# **1\. Introduction**

The global wildfire crisis is worsening in terms of economic impact (Smith, 2020), property destruction (CAL FIRE et al., 2023\), and loss of life (Smith, 2025\). Climate change and the growing Wildland-Urban Interface (WUI) are expected to contribute to this crisis (Jolly et al., 2015; Radeloff et al., 2018; Schug et al., 2023\). In the WUI, research shows that some drivers of structure loss can be mitigated by residents, such as near home fuel reduction called defensible space and using fire resistant building materials called home hardening. Together defensible space and home hardening are called the Home Ignition Zone. (). Governments (for example, the State of California) and insurers (for example, the insurance Institute for Business and Home Safety, or IBHS) have responded by establishing codes and standards requiring fire hazard mitigation on private land (CAL FIRE le-100, 202x?; IBHS, 202x?). 

In WUI communities, in-person inspections for the required mitigations are often inaccurate and inspection goals fall short as well; for example, CAL FIRE only inspected 123 of their 250k goal in 2024.CAL FIRE has fallen short of its yearly goal to inspect 250k of the state’s 750k WUI properties (Board of Forestry and Fire Protection, 2024\), and IBHS charges consumers for inspections to certify compliance with their standards (ref?). Airplane- and satellite-based remote sensing methods are used by insurers (cite Zesty, Verisk), but they often lack the resolution to accurately resolve the critical 0-5 ft zone and small, policy relevant hazards hazards (e.g. trash cans, propane tanks, vehicles, and others). 

combustible materials within the five-foot perimeter of a structure are among the strongest predictors of ignition ([Hedayati et al., 2018](https://ibhs.org/wp-content/uploads/member_docs/Near-Building_Noncombustible_Zone_Report_IBHS.pdf); [Zamanialaei et al., 2025](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-63386-2)). Vehicles parked against structures, propane tanks in dry vegetation, plastic trash cans left in Zone 0, and exposed wood piles are all regulated hazards under [California PRC 4291](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?division=4.&chapter=3.&part=2.&lawCode=PRC) and the [IBHS Wildfire Prepared Home standards](https://wildfireprepared.org/wp-content/uploads/WFPH-Technical-Standard.pdf).

Improvements to Uncrewed Aerial Vehicle (UAV) technology, or drones, promise to increase the resolution and accessibility of remote sensing of the HIZ (Brillon et al., 2026\). UAVs offer very high spatial resolution, typically 1-4 cm Ground Sampling Distance (GSD), and they are less expensive and easier to deploy than airplanes or satellites, although their spatial coverage is smaller and limited by legal, operational, and social factors. Artificial Intelligence (AI) models for land cover classification and object detection have also improved recently, promising faster and more accurate interpretation of remotely-sensed imagery (refs?).

This study proposes a framework for continued development of AI models to detect fire hazards and mitigations based in the CAL FIRE Le 100A () and the IBHS WIldfire Prepared Home program () using UAV imagery collected for a previous study (Brillon et al., 2026\) . For the first time, we automate the detection of small, policy-relevant objects such as trash cans, propane tanks, and vehicles, to answer three research questions. 

**RQ1.** Can a multimodal Visual Learning Model (VLM) identify trash cans, propane tanks, and vehicles?

**RQ2.** Does injecting structured California regulations and Insurance Institute for Business and Home Safety standards  into the model's reasoning context improve detection accuracy and compliance judgment compared to a plain visual prompt?

**RQ3.** Across GPT-4o Vision, Claude Vision, and GeoChat-7B, how do different VLMs compare on fire hazards, mitigation, and compliance assessment, and where do their failure modes differ in ways that matter for real-world deployment?

# **2.1 Study Sites and Data**

The 45 consent-approved drone images used in this study were collected during 2024 HIZ survey flights at the same five sites (Brillon et al., submitted): Felton (N \= 9), Redwood Estates (N \= 10), and Saratoga (N \= 8\) in the Santa Cruz Mountains, and Paradise (N \= 10\) and Tahoe Donner (N \= 10\) in the Sierra Nevada Mountains. All are in high or very high Fire Hazard Severity Zones under California PRC 4291\.

Images were captured using a DJI Phantom 4 V2 at 400 feet altitude with 90 to 95 percent image overlap, producing true-color orthomosaics at 1 to 3 cm ground sampling distance . At this resolution, vehicles, trash cans, propane tanks, and wood piles are clearly distinguishable from the surrounding context. Each property also has an in-situ assessment record from the evaluation form used in [Wilkin et al., 2025](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijdrr.2025.105435), which documents the status of each inspection item as Satisfactory Condition, Needs Maintenance, Absent, or NA across Zones 0 through 100 feet. This forms the ground truth against which AI detections are evaluated.

# **2.2 Proof of Concept: What a Plain Prompt Revealed**

Before designing the full pipeline, a deliberate baseline test was run on one of the 45 drone images using **Claude Sonnet 4.6** (Anthropic, March 2026\) with no prior context, no regulatory framing, and no few-shot examples. Claude Sonnet 4.6 is a multimodal large language model capable of processing both image and text inputs simultaneously. It can describe what it sees in a photograph, reason spatially about the relationships between objects, and produce structured text output. The intent of this test was to determine what a capable commercial VLM could identify from a WUI drone image without any task-specific guidance, establishing a clear before-and-after contrast that motivates the full pipeline design.

![][image1]

*Figure 1\. Sample drone image (DJI\_0697.JPG) from the 2024 Wilkin/GeoFly Lab HIZ survey flights used in the zero-shot baseline test. Resolution is approximately 2 to 3 cm GSD. Multiple structures, vehicles, and tree canopies overhanging rooflines are visible.*

The image (Figure 1\) shows a residential WUI neighborhood captured at nadir from approximately 400 feet altitude. Claude Sonnet 4.6 was shown this image with the instruction: describe what you see, with no additional context. The response it produced is shown below exactly as returned:

| *The overall scene is a residential neighborhood photographed from directly above. The image* *covers roughly 6 to 10 residential parcels. The soil color, dry golden-brown grass, and sparse* *green tree canopy immediately suggest a hot, dry climate — California foothills or similar.* *Structures: at least 7 distinct rooftops. Most appear to be dark gray asphalt shingles, with at* *least one solar panel array visible near the top center. A large white vehicle — likely a van or* *pickup — is parked near the cul-de-sac. At least two darker-colored cars are visible near* *structures. Shadow geometry is short and sharp, consistent with a midday flight.* *Vegetation: green trees cluster unevenly — some parcels have dense canopy overhanging* *rooflines, others have almost none. Several areas show dry reddish-brown exposed soil and dead* *grass. A large area of exposed bare red-orange soil in the center-left appears recently disturbed.* *What I cannot determine: roof material beyond color, anything under tree canopy shadows,* *vent screen sizes, siding material, and vertical clearance measurements. A cylindrical object* *near the lower-center right may be a propane tank or water tank — I cannot confirm without* *zooming in. Two houses have tree canopies that appear to extend over or very close to their* *rooflines. That pattern registers as a risk even without fire safety training.* |
| :---- |

The model correctly identified the presence of vehicles, approximate roof material class, tree canopy overhang against rooflines, dry versus live ground cover, and the presence of a potential propane tank as a candidate object. It also identified exactly what it could not determine from a nadir view: anything under canopy, vent details, siding material, and vertical clearance measurements. This boundary maps closely to the 'Questions Related to UAV' categorization already compiled by the lab team, which is itself an independent validation of the model's self-assessment.

The limitation is equally telling. The model produced a useful visual description but had no way to connect any observation to a regulatory consequence. It could see the white cylindrical object. It could not connect that sighting to the PRC 4291 requirement for 10 feet of bare mineral soil and 10 additional feet of no flammable vegetation. That connection requires the regulatory context to be injected into the prompt, which is the exact problem the Graph-RAG and few-shot chain-of-thought approach in this paper solves.

## **2.3  Knowledge Graph Construction**

The knowledge graph is built from PRC 4291, the IBHS Wildfire Prepared Home standards, and the lab's evaluation taxonomy sheet. It is implemented as a Python NetworkX structure where nodes represent combustible object classes and directed edges represent regulatory relationships. A propane\_tank node connects to a 10-foot bare mineral soil rule, which connects to a second node requiring no flammable vegetation for an additional 10 feet. A vehicle node connects to the IBHS prohibition on parking within 5 feet of a structure. When the VLM detects an object, the pipeline traverses the graph from that node and injects the full compliance rule chain into the next prompt. This is what distinguishes Graph-RAG from a plain keyword lookup ([ARPaCCino, arXiv:2507.10584](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.10584)).

### **Prompt structure**

| SYSTEM: You are a wildfire defensible space compliance assessor evaluating drone imagery against California PRC 4291 and IBHS Wildfire Prepared Home standards. Work through each step before producing any verdict. Cite the specific clause that applies. REGULATORY CONTEXT \[from knowledge graph\]:   Propane tank: PRC 4291 — 10 ft bare mineral soil around tank     plus additional 10 ft with no flammable vegetation.   Vehicle: IBHS — no vehicle within 5 ft of structure.   Trash can: plastic in Zone 0 (0-5 ft) is a combustible hazard.     Metal containers are acceptable. FEW-SHOT EXAMPLE (propane tank, Zone 0, violation):   PERCEIVE: Cylindrical silver object, \~28px diameter at GSD     2.5cm/px \= \~70cm real diameter. Shadow \~14px \= \~35cm height.     Morphology matches residential propane tank.   LOCATE: \~4 feet from south wall of structure. Zone 0 (0-5 ft).   RETRIEVE: PRC 4291 requires 10 ft bare mineral soil around     propane tank. Dry grass visible within required clearance.   ASSESS: VIOLATION. Zone 0 weight x3. Confidence: HIGH. USER: \[image tile attached\] OUTPUT: JSON — object\_class, bounding\_box\_pixels \[x1,y1,x2,y2\],   zone, compliance\_status, confidence, cot\_trace. |
| :---- |

For borderline cases, a self-consistency layer submits the same prompt three times and takes the majority verdict ([Wang et al., 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.11171)). This improves reliability on ambiguous visual inputs without any additional model training.

# **5\. Discussion**

## **5.1 UAV-Based HIZ Assessment**

Henri’s manuscript is the direct predecessor. That manuscript automates land cover classification using Random Forest on four-band UAV imagery (RGB \+ canopy height model), achieving 63 percent overall accuracy (Cohen's Kappa \= 0.55), and evaluates compliance with selected CAL FIRE and IBHS vegetation standards. Its Appendix A policy analysis categorizes manmade combustible objects including vehicles, boats, RVs, and trash cans as UAV-detectable but does not automate them. This paper takes on exactly those objects.

Stevens et al. (in preparation) use airborne LiDAR and individual tree crown segmentation via the dalponte2016 algorithm in lidR to model vertical vegetation structure and canopy base height. Together with [Wilkin et al., 2025](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijdrr.2025.105435), the three manuscripts form an integrated automated HIZ assessment program spanning vegetation structure, land cover, and manmade combustible objects.

# **Appendix**

## **Appendix A. Methods**

### **2.4 Image Tiling and Bounding Box Detection**

Each orthomosaic is tiled into overlapping 512-pixel patches. The pipeline first detects the primary building footprint using [Grounding DINO (Liu et al., 2023\)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.05499) and computes pixel-distance zone buffers at the known GSD. Tiles within Zone 0 receive denser overlap sampling. Grounding DINO is then run with text queries for each object class ('trash can', 'propane tank', 'vehicle', 'wood pile') and produces candidate bounding boxes. For cases needing pixel-level boundary detail, [SAM 2 (Ravi et al., 2024\)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.00714) generates segmentation masks within each box.

The final annotated output draws colored bounding boxes on the original orthomosaic: red for confirmed violations, green for compliant conditions, and yellow for cases where confidence falls below the threshold and human review is recommended. The VLM is instructed to return bounding box pixel coordinates as a structured JSON field alongside each compliance verdict, and a post-processing script converts those coordinates into the visual annotations.

### **2.5 Prompting Strategy: Few-Shot Chain-of-Thought**

As the zero-shot baseline in Section 3 showed, a plain visual prompt produces useful description but cannot connect visual observations to regulatory consequences. The full pipeline uses **few-shot chain-of-thought prompting** ([Wei et al., 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.11903)), where each inference call includes two worked demonstration examples before the actual image is presented. Each example walks through four named steps drawn from [Geo-CoT (Liu et al., arXiv:2509.22221)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.22221): Perceive, Locate, Retrieve, and Assess.

In the Perceive step, the model describes the visual evidence at specific coordinates including object morphology, shadow geometry, and approximate dimensions from the known GSD. In the Locate step, it estimates the defensible space zone by referencing the pre-drawn buffer lines. In the Retrieve step, it cites the specific PRC 4291 or IBHS clause from the injected knowledge graph context. In the Assess step, it produces the compliance verdict with a confidence rating and a follow-up recommendation if warranted.

### **2.6 Multi-Model Comparison**

The same pipeline runs across three VLMs: [GPT-4o Vision](https://openai.com/index/hello-gpt-4o/) as the primary commercial model, [Claude Sonnet 4.6](https://www.anthropic.com) as the secondary commercial model, and [GeoChat-7B (Kuckreja et al., 2024\)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.15826) as the open-source RS-specialized baseline. An ablation study runs every image through each model both with and without the Graph-RAG context injection, isolating its contribution to accuracy and compliance judgment independently of each model's visual capabilities.

### **2.7 Evaluation**

All 45 images are manually annotated in [Label Studio](https://labelstud.io) for the three target object classes, with Grounding DINO pre-populating candidate boxes. The 70/30 development and held-out test split ensure that reported metrics reflect generalization rather than prompt overfitting. Precision, recall, and F1 are computed per object class. Cohen's kappa measures compliance verdict agreement between AI output and in-situ records. A parcel-level weighted compliance score (Zone 0 weight x3, Zone 1 x2, Zone 2 x1) is correlated with the inspector-derived score using Pearson r.

# **Idea parking garage**

## **5.2 Multimodal VLMs in Remote Sensing**

[GeoChat (Kuckreja et al., 2024\)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.15826) is the first VLM trained specifically for remote sensing visual question answering. Surveys by [Huang et al. (arXiv:2503.22081)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.22081) and [Weng et al. (arXiv:2505.14361)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.14361) review this landscape and identify explanation-driven model reliability as a key open research direction. No prior work applies RS VLMs to WUI residential combustible object detection or HIZ compliance checking.

## **5.3 RAG-Grounded Regulatory Compliance**

[Sun et al. (ACL/COLING 2025\)](https://aclanthology.org/) propose a three-layer retrieval-augmented generation framework for building code compliance. [ARPaCCino (arXiv:2507.10584)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.10584) combines LLMs, RAG, and tool-based validation to translate natural language policy into formal compliance rules. This paper adapts that architectural pattern for aerial HIZ imagery using a lightweight knowledge graph.

## **5.4 Chain-of-Thought Prompting and Geospatial Explainability**

[Wei et al. (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.11903) establish that few-shot chain-of-thought prompting reliably improves accuracy and interpretability over direct-answer prompting across complex reasoning tasks. [Liu et al. (arXiv:2509.22221)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.22221) introduce Geo-CoT, a geospatial chain-of-thought framework where spatial claims are anchored to specific image references. A companion study ([arXiv:2511.11198](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.11198)) shows that CoT supervision improves RS VQA accuracy by 34.9 percent over direct-answer baselines. A systematic XAI review ([arXiv:2402.13791](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.13791)) documents a roughly 70-fold gap between ML and explainability papers in Earth observation, motivating this study's use of CoT as a built-in audit trail.
